node_repl on gateway rows

node_repl (browser, Chrome and computer use) on gateway rows: native evidence, how auto review runs in gateway executors, rules, model switching and the check script.

About 13 min read · 6 sections

On this page
01 Evidence 02 How review runs in gateway executors 03 Rules 04 Switching models during a running turn 05 What the desktop shows 06 Check script

node_repl runs the browser, Chrome and computer-use tools. Gateway chats get the same node_repl capability and the same safety policy as native rows, and never a weaker one. This guide owns the details, because app-server.md was already over 500 lines on main; the Codex 2 rows section of that guide summarizes them. The code is in src/auto-review.ts, src/codex-native-rows.ts, src/desktop-catalog.ts and src/server.ts.

Evidence

The SDK reads the policy from the ModelInfo fields node_repl_disabled, node_repl_auto_review_required, guardian and auto_review_model_override. The runtime source is the client's own ~/.codex/models_cache.json (client 0.162.0, fetched 2026-10-15), which the adapter loads as the native catalog. It was read-only observed, together with the bundled plugins, ~/.codex/config.toml and the Codex source (ModelInfo in codex-rs/protocol, pinned revision 740e5af):

  • node_repl does not depend on code mode. The bundled unified-computer-use plugin declares cua_repl with omit_tools_from: ["code_mode", "deferred"], and ~/.codex/config.toml runs [mcp_servers.node_repl] from the app. Only tool_mode follows code mode.
  • A gateway executor selects tool mode from the executable that starts that generation. If its selected gateway SDK receipt names no executable, verified codex-code-mode-host beside that executable, every executor catalog row explicitly uses tool_mode: "direct", including rows whose native metadata omitted or used an unknown tool mode. Direct mode overrides Code Mode feature flags, so it runs normal tools without attempting to start a missing host. This does not change node_repl, permissions, review, instructions, or the native engine's own catalog.
  • Every native row has node_repl_disabled: false. gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-sol set node_repl_auto_review_required: true; gpt-6-luna, gpt-reserve, the 5.6 rows and gpt-daybreak-blue-latest set it to false. guardian, auto_review_model_override and requires_sandboxed_review are absent on every row in that file, and the SDK reads an absent field as null. The catalog embedded in the ChatGPT.app codex binary states them instead: guardian and auto_review_model_override are null and requires_sandboxed_review is false on its rows. The two sources mean the same. requires_sandboxed_review is data only: it is not a ModelInfo field in the pinned source (only the bundled models-manager/models.json names it), and in both the ChatGPT.app codex and the gateway SDK binary it appears only inside the embedded catalog, never among the fields their parser reads.
  • In the SDK, ModelInfo::computer_use_review_required lets a guardian policy, when one is set, decide review instead of the flag: computer use is reviewed unless guardian.computer_use is absent, null or disabled. A null guardian leaves the flag in charge. A missing node_repl field means false.
  • The hidden row codex-auto-review is the reviewer: visibility: hide, supported_in_api: true, use_responses_lite: true, and its model_messages.auto_review holds policy, policy_template and node_repl_policy, which is the node_repl review text. The four 6.x rows set auto_review.rejection_instructions (the same 388-character text on all four) and leave policy, policy_template and timeout_instructions null.
  • Only gpt-daybreak-blue-latest sets model_specialty: "cyber". In the SDK that selects a stricter Guardian rejection policy (the turn is interrupted after one denial instead of three consecutive or ten recent ones) and ignores prefix rules.
  • The four 6.x rows share one confirmation_policies and one guardian_v2 (identical across the rows). Rows such as gpt-5.6-luna have neither. Claude, Copilot and Qwen rows are published by the gateway and have neither either.

How review runs in gateway executors

An action that needs review goes to a reviewer model. The SDK chooses it as follows (core/src/guardian/reviewer_config.rs, ext/guardian-reviewer/src/model.rs):

  1. The default reviewer is approval_review_preferred_model() of the turn provider: gpt-5.6-luna only when the provider has cached API-key auth, otherwise codex-auto-review.
  2. A gateway executor's provider authenticates with auth.command, so the SDK builds a fresh external-bearer AuthManager for it whose cache starts empty. Nothing reads auth through the turn provider (the model client and the extensions build their own providers), so the cache stays empty and the default is codex-auto-review. gpt-5.6-luna is never selected from an executor.
  3. The row's own auto_review_model_override, when set, replaces the default.
  4. The chosen reviewer is used only if its row is in the executor's model list. That list is filtered for API-key auth, so the row needs supported_in_api: true. Otherwise the SDK falls back to the parent model, with the parent's own messages. That is not the native review, so the catalog must never allow it: a reviewer row that is missing or not supported_in_api: true keeps node_repl off.
  5. The review text is the SDK's own: the instructions and node_repl policy come from the reviewer row's model_messages.auto_review, plus the SDK's output contract. The gateway adds, removes and rewrites no review text.

The reviewer is a normal thread on the same gateway provider. It never executes anything for the client: its tools (exec_command, write_stdin, view_image, exec and wait) run read-only inside the SDK's sandbox, so the reviewer may inspect state with read-only commands. Full Access approves the empty-schema node_repl elicitations without any review, as natively. So does the user approvals reviewer, for ordinary node_repl js calls that are not sensitive and need no user input (core/src/session/mcp.rs, user_cua_execution).

A live check of the pinned gateway SDK, with a fake gateway and no paid inference, saw the reviewer request as POST /v1/responses with model: "codex-auto-review", reasoning.effort: "low", text.format.type: "json_schema", store: false, stream: true, include, prompt_cache_key, client_metadata and tool_choice; input items additional_tools, two developer messages and user messages; and no service_tier. With the reviewer row removed from the catalog, the same action sent the reviewer request under the parent model instead.

The reviewer route

The gateway serves exactly one reviewer slug, codex-auto-review (src/auto-review.ts), through the Codex subscription provider, and never gpt-5.6-luna.

  • Resolution is: an alias with that exact name, then the bare-model alias rule (nativeModelAlias), then the Codex provider designated with "defaultForBareModels": true, or the sole Codex subscription when none is designated. With no Codex provider, or several without an alias or a designated default, the request gets 404 model_not_found and no other provider is called.
  • The request reaches the same adapter instance as that provider's own rows, so the credential, turn state and reasoning scope match. The body is passed on unchanged apart from the model, as for any Codex route. /v1/models does not list it.
  • GET /v1/model-catalog adds auto_review: { "models": ["codex-auto-review"] } only when that route resolves to a Codex subscription provider with a stored plan login (hasPlanLogin: scopes present; no refresh, no network, no write). Any error omits the field. Older adapters ignore the extra key, and so does Codex's ModelsResponse.
  • The upstream accepting the slug on the subscription endpoint was not verified live: the only stored login was expired, and refreshing it would rotate the installed credential. Until a call is checked, a rejected slug shows as failed reviews (below), not as a wrong answer.

The desktop adapter

The adapter turns node_repl on for a row that needs review only when all of these hold: the last successful live read of the catalog advertised the row's reviewer slug (its auto_review_model_override, or codex-auto-review when none), and the native catalog carries that reviewer row with supported_in_api: true. A restored cache, a start without a read, a source change or an older gateway means no advertisement, so those rows have node_repl off until a read succeeds. A failed refresh keeps the last snapshot. The reviewers are part of the catalog revision, so a change starts a new executor generation.

Scope, data and decision

The route serves every Auto-review approval in a gateway executor, not only node_repl. The SDK resolves the reviewer the same way for node_repl elicitations, shell and exec escalations, apply_patch, network access, MCP tool calls and permission requests (core/src/tools/approvals.rs, orchestrator.rs, network_approval.rs, runtimes/unified_exec.rs, core/src/session/mcp.rs). The gateway cannot tell these apart without reading request bodies, which it never does. Only chats whose approvals reviewer is Auto-review send reviews.

On 0.3.9 each of these reviews got 404 from the gateway, and the SDK counts a failed review as a denial, so every action that needed Auto-review was declined in gateway chats. Now those actions and their transcript context go to OpenAI's reviewer through the Codex subscription; for Claude, Copilot and Qwen chats they leave that chat's own provider. Edi decided on 2026-10-15 that the route is on: gateway engines send the review step to OpenAI's reviewer through the Codex subscription, and it fails closed only when that route is unavailable. The review text is never logged: telemetry records fixed fields only, and no token, prompt, request body, tool argument or environment value is logged.

Telemetry

Every Auto-review request (any kind, above) carries autoReview: true, with model set to that slug, on request_completed, request_empty and request_failed, including the 404. gateway diagnostics adds an autoReview bucket: completed, empty and failed:<code>. Other model names are never recorded for a request without a route.

Rules

  • A Codex 2 row copies node_repl_disabled, node_repl_auto_review_required, guardian, auto_review_model_override, requires_sandboxed_review (data only, see Evidence) and model_specialty from its native row, with code mode on or off. A value that is not plainly typed is not copied, and a node_repl field that is not a boolean becomes true.
  • A row needs review when its guardian reviews computer use, or when it has no guardian and its flag is not plainly false. A guardian that is not an object counts as needing review. Such a row has node_repl on only if its reviewer runs (see above); otherwise node_repl is off, so no action waits on a reviewer that fails. With the live config and the route advertised, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra and gpt-6-sol keep it on with review, and rows such as gpt-6-luna and the 5.6 rows keep it on without review.
  • The native rows that the executor catalog carries for sub-agents naming a model directly follow the same rule as the Codex 2 row for that model, so one upstream model has one policy in an executor. A native row that states no node_repl policy gets node_repl off there. The reviewer row keeps its node_repl and review fields. Every carried row has the tool search flag off, whatever the native row says: a bare model name resolves to a route only when the request runs, and that route may drop tool_search rather than bridge it. A gateway alias spelled like a native slug, which could take that name first, is refused at launch. The native engine's own catalog is unchanged. No row's messages are rewritten.
  • A row with no native counterpart (Claude, Copilot, Qwen, API, or a Codex row whose upstream is missing) always requires review, the strictest policy, and carries no guardian. Its confirmation_policies and guardian_v2 come from the native rows: when a text is on several native rows and all values are equal (as JSON), it is copied; when a text is on none, it is left out; when the values differ, nothing is shared and node_repl is off. Without these texts node_repl would read an empty openai/confirmation_policies, which clears the connector defaults. node_repl is off if the reviewer does not run, any native row turns it off or states no policy, or there is no native catalog. requires_sandboxed_review: true is carried when a native row sets it, as data only; nothing enforces it.
  • A guardian on any native row turns node_repl off for every fallback row, with code mode on or off. A fallback row cannot mirror a guardian (its computer-use mode, scoring, or shell, MCP, network and permission scopes), so a review policy that may differ from the strictest native one is never applied; off is the stricter choice. No native row sets a guardian today.
  • Fallback rows do not copy auto_review.rejection_instructions, so a denied action in a Claude, Copilot, Qwen, API or missing-upstream chat shows the SDK's bundled rejection guidance, as the 5.6 rows do natively. It is stricter than the 6.x text: it tells the agent to stop and request user input, where the 6.x text lets it finish unaffected work.
  • The plain catalog (CLI and remote clients) publishes true for both fields on every row.
  • Executors start on the machine with the native catalog and settings. Their config.toml is written from the native config/read settings, and the gateway drops only provider, login, API key and catalog keys, not mcp_servers, so the node_repl server resolves as it does natively.

Fails closed

Any one of these turns node_repl off for the rows that need review, and for fallback rows:

  • no live catalog read yet, or a gateway too old to send the field;
  • no Codex subscription route, or several without an alias or a designated default;
  • no ChatGPT plan login on the reviewer provider;
  • the reviewer row missing from the native catalog, or supported_in_api not exactly true;
  • an override that names a slug the gateway does not advertise, or is not a string;
  • native rows that disagree on a shared review text, any native row that turns node_repl off, or any native row that sets a guardian (fallback rows only).

The adapter does not know a chat's approvals reviewer, so review-required rows stay off without an advertised reviewer even when that chat would not use the reviewer (Full Access or the user approvals reviewer).

At run time any reviewer failure (401, 404, 5xx, timeout) makes the SDK decline the action. In a mixed deployment an inference host older than this release sends no auto_review, so those rows stay off until the host is updated.

Switching models during a running turn

This is the SDK's behaviour, not the gateway's. check_legacy_model_safety (core/src/session/step_activation.rs) rejects turn/settings/update with a model when the destination differs from the running turn in node_repl_disabled, computer_use_review_required, guardian, auto_review_model_override, the cyber specialty, the guardian_v2 settings (with the feature or a guardian), or the parent-fallback review texts. App-server maps the rejection to JSON-RPC -32600 with the SDK's reason. The router forwards it unchanged and records the new model only for an applied result, so the turn keeps its model.

On the live configuration (the guardianv2 feature off, its default) the rows fall in three groups, and a mid-turn switch works only inside one. With guardianv2 on, the guardian_v2 settings are compared too, so gpt-6-luna, which carries them, no longer switches with the 5.6 rows:

Group Rows
Review required gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol, every Claude, Copilot and Qwen row
Review not required gpt-6-luna, gpt-reserve, the 5.6 rows
Cyber (model_specialty) gpt-daybreak-blue-latest

Claude to gpt-6.1-sol still switches mid-turn; Claude to gpt-6-luna is rejected, like native gpt-6.1-sol to gpt-6-luna, and a switch to or from gpt-daybreak-blue-latest is rejected like natively (the destination changes the admitted Guardian rejection policy). The groups are the same with or without the reviewer. thread/settings/update changes the next turn and is never checked.

ChatGPT desktop 26.1007 changes the model only through thread/settings/update and sends turn/settings/update only with approvalsReviewer. The picker therefore never hits the rejection: it shows the new model, the running turn finishes on the old one, and the next turn uses the new one. A CLI or script gets the error. With midTurnModelSwitch on, the adapter offers the picker change to the running turn and keeps the next-turn behaviour when this check refuses it (mid-turn model changes).

What the desktop shows

  • Browser, Chrome and computer-use tools appear on a gateway row when its reviewer is advertised, and for rows that need no review.
  • Reviews appear as the native Auto-review items (item/autoApprovalReview/started and completed), forwarded from the executor.
  • A failed review declines the action and is counted under autoReview in gateway diagnostics.
  • If the route is unavailable, review-required rows have no browser for that executor generation.

Check script

node scripts/check-node-repl.mjs <copy> reads a copy of a combined catalog: <stateDirectory>/desktop-catalog-<revision>.json, which one executor generation loads as model_catalog_json, or <stateDirectory>/desktop-models.json, which holds the latest one once the adapter has restored or refreshed. It prints both node_repl fields for every row as JSON, and guardian when one is set. It then counts the rows that keep node_repl off and the rows that enable it without review, as the SDK reads them: a missing node_repl_disabled means enabled, and a set guardian decides review. A guardian that is not an object, or a computer_use mode that is not a string, counts as without review. The last line reports the reviewer row codex-auto-review: missing, or its supported_in_api and whether its node_repl_policy is present. The script is advisory and exits 0, also for unreadable or malformed input. Pass it a copy, never the installed app's live state.
